 Final 2026 midterm election results: Democrats clinch 56-seat Senate majority with Peltola's Alaska win. What they can — and can't — do next.
 President Trump enjoyed complete Republican control of Congress for the first half of his second term. Not anymore.
 Andrew Romano , Mike Bebernes Updated Fri, November 20, 2026 at 10:11 PM UTC 8 min read Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google. A Jackson State University student voter holds up a Mississippi "I Voted 2026" sticker after casting a ballot at Jackson State University on Nov. 3, 2026. (Aron Smith/Jackson State University via Getty Images) With Mary Peltola's victory in Alaska on Tuesday night , Democrats officially flipped their ninth U.S. Senate seat of the 2026 midterm elections — the most in nearly 70 years . When the next Congress takes office in early January, the Democratic Party will boast its largest Senate majority since 2011, with 56 seats to the GOP's 44. 
 Though a few races remain too close to call, the dust has mostly settled on Democrats' 2026 landslide. Their sweeping victories in the U.S. House, Senate and statehouses nationwide add up to the biggest "blue wave" since Watergate .
 The question now is what Democrats plan to do with their newfound power. On Wednesday, the party nominated New York Rep. Hakeem Jeffries for House speaker, putting him on track to be the first Black American to wield the gavel. With a majority that could top out at 260 seats after the last votes are counted — the largest for either party since the early 1990s  — Jeffries will have enormous leeway to send new legislation to the Senate while also blocking parts of President Trump's agenda, investigating his administration and possibly even impeaching him (again) . 
 Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement On the Senate side, Democratic stalwart Chuck Schumer of New York will compete with Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen for the role of majority leader. Whoever wins the party's internal battle — which is expected to drag on for weeks — will control which policies are emphasized, which bills are brought to the floor, when votes occur, which judges and appointees are confirmed and how all of this is communicated to the president and the public. 
 Among the priorities under discussion on both sides of the aisle: reinstating Affordable Care Act subsidies that expired under the previous Republican Congress; reversing nearly $1 trillion in recent GOP Medicaid cuts; expanding Medicare by lowering the eligibility age and adding vision, hearing and dental coverage; addressing the high prices of groceries and other goods by blocking Trump's global tariffs and restoring congressional power over trade policy; cutting off Iran war funding; and launching investigations of ICE, presidential pardons, political pressure on federal law enforcement, the Epstein files and the Trump family's business dealings. 
 As for impeachment, Rep. Jamie Raskin, a Democrat from Maryland who is set to chair the House Judiciary Committee, told Punchbowl that it's a "critical tool in the constitutional toolbox" — but far from a sure thing. "We will not hesitate to use it if we think that the benefits exceed the costs," Raskin said. "But the one thing everybody's well aware of is that impeachment trials and impeachment motions soak up a lot of energy and oxygen."
 Despite their sizable House and Senate majorities, Democrats will be limited in what legislation they can pass into law. Trump still has veto power, and Senate Republicans still hold enough seats to filibuster most bills. Meanwhile, many incoming Democratic lawmakers (like Peltola) are relative moderates representing red states and districts — meaning the party will have to calibrate its approach carefully to keep them on board and maximize its chances of winning the 2028 elections.
 Advertisement Advertisement Beyond Washington, D.C., Democrats will now control the governorship and both legislative houses in six new states: Arizona, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, Nevada, Michigan and Minnesota. They will also hold the majority in a dozen new statehouse chambers. As a result, the party will have more opportunities to experiment with new policy ideas, approve congressional maps, influence election procedures, fill Senate vacancies and help a new generation of governors build executive experience ahead of future presidential elections. 
 It's even possible that state Democratic leaders could change the way we elect our next president by sidestepping the Electoral College and preventing candidates from winning the White House without winning the popular vote .
 How many Senate seats did Democrats win?
 Democrats came into the midterms needing a net gain of four seats to win back the Senate. To do that, they had to defend a handful of potentially vulnerable swing-state seats while also flipping at least a few seats in historically red states. 
 That's exactly what happened. Republican efforts to flip blue seats in Michigan, Georgia, Minnesota and New Hampshire all came up well short. Meanwhile, Democrats won nine GOP-held seats in Mississippi, Maine, Texas, South Carolina, Ohio, North Carolina, Iowa, Kansas and, as of Tuesday night, Alaska. 
 Advertisement Advertisement Only two incumbent Republican senators in competitive races were able to win reelection: Florida's Ashley Moody and Nebraska's Pete Ricketts.
 The last undecided race was called late Tuesday night, as Mary Peltola defeated incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan to become the first Alaska Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate since 2008.
 Peltola secured just over 50% of the vote, narrowly clearing the threshold required to win without triggering Alaska's unique ranked choice voting system.
 Democrats will enter 2027 with 56 seats in the Senate .
 How many House seats did Democrats win?
 So far, Democrats have won 257 U.S. House seats — far more than the 218 they needed for a majority. That includes 46 red-to-blue flips. Democrats' 14-point victory in the House popular vote is the largest in any midterm since 1974. 
 Advertisement Advertisement Races that were too close to call on Election Night have been decided in the days that followed.
 Last Thursday, Republicans flipped Maine's 2nd District , where a conservative Democrat had retired — and where former GOP Gov. Paul LePage officially defeated Matt Dunlap, the progressive state auditor, by more than 5,000 votes after ranked-choice tabulation. Dunlap conceded to LePage on Nov. 5. It was the third seat to flip to the GOP this midterm cycle.
 Last Friday, GOP firebrand Lauren Boebert lost her reelection battle in Colorado's 4th District — long considered one of the state's safest Republican seats — to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired rear admiral in the Navy. After a close 2022 reelection fight in her previous district, Boebert switched to the 4th District for her 2024 campaign and won by about 11 percentage points. Laubacher's lead — about 3,400 votes — was too big to trigger an automatic recount.
 Later that day, Democrat Eric Jones unseated Democratic Rep. Mike Thompson in California's 4th District, where only Democrats were on the ballot under the state's top-two system.
 Advertisement Advertisement On Monday, Republican Reps. David Rouzer and Jay Obernolte narrowly won reelection to North Carolina's 7th District and California's 23rd District , respectively.
 Democrats flipped another GOP-held seat on Tuesday, when Raymond Smith was declared the winner in North Carolina's 3rd District. Smith prevailed by fewer than 300 votes. Alaska's at-large seat was called the next day, with incumbent Republican Nick Begich securing reelection. On Friday, Republican Pat Harrigan won reelection in North Carolina's 10th Congressional District after Democrat Ashley Bell conceded. (Bell, who trailed by about 2,500 votes, requested a recount last week.)
 Where things stand in the undecided House races 
 Five U.S. House races remain unresolved.
 Advertisement Advertisement Two are in Louisiana, where the top two finishers in the 5th and 6th Districts will meet in a Dec. 12 runoff.
 Meanwhile, Democrats hold narrow leads in lead in races for three Republican-held seats (as of Friday afternoon). In Tennessee's 4th District , Victoria Broderick leads Rep. Scott DesJarlais by about 270 votes. In Minnesota's 1st District , Jake Johnson leads Rep. Brad Finstad by about 320 votes; Finstad has requested a recount . In North Carolina's 5th District , Chuck Hubbard leads Rep. Virginia Foxx by about 330 votes.
 North Carolina certifies results on Nov. 24.
 How many governorships did Democrats win?
 Republican governors have outnumbered their Democratic counterparts for the last 15 years straight (and for 26 of the last 30 years overall). But this year, Democrats have reversed the "governor gap," flipping six governorships in Iowa, Texas, Ohio, Nevada, Alaska and Georgia to bring their total to 30 — the party's first gubernatorial majority since 2011.
 Advertisement Advertisement On Thursday, Democrats also held onto Kansas , where voters elected Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher to become the Sunflower State's fourth woman governor ever. She defeated Republican Ty Masterson, the state's Senate president.
 "Kansans have sent a clear message that they want to keep our state moving forward," Holscher said in a video posted online Tuesday. "The work of preparing to lead has already begun."
 The AP called Alaska's governor race for Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins early Saturday. He won a majority of first-choice votes, so no ranked-choice count was needed. He will be the state's first Democratic governor since Tony Knowles left office in 2002, and he takes office Dec. 7.
 How many state legislatures did Democrats win? 
 Democrats' gains were also seen at the state level. They flipped more than 500 state legislative seats across the country and turned a total of 12 legislative chambers blue.
 Advertisement Advertisement That includes three states where they flipped both chambers: Arizona, New Hampshire and Wisconsin. After Election Day's results, Democrats will control the House, Senate and governorship in Arizona for the first time since 1966. Democrats also secured a "trifecta" in Wisconsin. They'll hold both legislative chambers in New Hampshire, but the governorship in the Granite State will remain in Republican hands. 
 Democrats regained trifectas in Minnesota, Michigan and Pennsylvania by clinching majorities in the lone GOP-led chamber in their states. They flipped a single chamber in Georgia, North Carolina and Texas, ensuring that Democratic governors in those states won't face unified Republican opposition within their state legislatures. 
 Where things stand in the undecided state legislative races 
 As of Monday morning, only three state legislative chambers — the North Carolina Senate and both chambers in Alaska — remained undecided, according to the AP. A recount is possible in North Carolina, where Senate control hinges on one race.
